lead: Packing is the working surface of a packed absorber. It is a bed of shaped pieces or corrugated sheets that gives gas and liquid a large area to meet, with a low gas pressure drop. Three numbers describe a packing: specific surface a, void fraction ε and packing factor Fp. They decide how much solute can transfer and how hard the gas must push. Packed towers are used for CO₂ removal, refinery gas treating, ammonia scrubbing and odour control.
prereq: You need: interfacial area and mass-transfer coefficients (from Individual and overall mass transfer coefficients) and equilibrium and operating lines.

blocks.text: A packed absorber is a vertical shell filled with small shaped pieces or a corrugated sheet stack. Gas rises through the gaps; liquid wets the surface and falls. The wetted surface is where solute crosses from gas to liquid. Packing exists to create that surface with as little gas pressure drop as possible. Figure 3.6.1 shows the parts of the worked example's tower.

Three numbers describe a packing. Specific surface a is the surface area of the packing per unit volume of packed bed, in m²/m³. The wetted area, which is what actually transfers solute, is at most this value and falls below it when liquid channels or the packing is not fully wet. Void fraction ε is the empty volume divided by the bed volume, dimensionless. Packing factor Fp is an empirical number, in m⁻¹, that rises as the packing becomes smaller and more obstructive; it is the input to the pressure-drop correlation in Chapter 3.7.
a = A<sub>p</sub> / V<sub>bed</sub>      ε = V<sub>void</sub> / V<sub>bed</sub>
blocks.where: A<sub>p</sub> is the total surface area of the packing in m²; V<sub>bed</sub> is the packed-bed volume in m³; V<sub>void</sub> is the void volume in m³. The maximum interfacial area in a bed is A = a × V<sub>bed</sub>; the actual wetted area may be less.

items: Random packings are dumped dry and settle randomly: Raschig rings (hollow cylinders), Pall rings (rings with internal tabs), Berl saddles and Intalox saddles. Common nominal sizes are 25 mm, 38 mm and 50 mm.
Structured packings are stacks of corrugated sheets or wire gauze, with a fixed geometry and a high area per volume.
Material: ceramic for corrosive service, plastic for cheap low-temperature duty, metal for high capacity.

As nominal size rises, a falls: a 25 mm ring gives roughly 200 m²/m³ while a 50 mm ring gives roughly 100 m²/m³. ε usually lies between 0.6 and 0.95 for random packings and ordinary structured sheet packings; wire-gauze and very open structured packings reach about 0.95–0.98.

blocks.text: Plot pressure drop per metre of bed ΔP/Z against gas mass flux G. At low G the line is nearly straight and gentle. At the loading point the slope begins to rise: liquid starts to accumulate in the voids, and the gas must push through more liquid. At the flooding point the line turns almost vertical. Liquid is held up and blown back, the bed cannot pass the flows, and operation becomes unstable.

More liquid fills more of the voids, so a higher liquid rate floods at a lower gas rate. Absorbers are commonly designed at 50 to 70 % of the flooding gas mass flux, read at the design liquid rate, and for a pressure drop of about 15 to 50 mm of water per metre of packing. Below the loading point the liquid hold-up hardly depends on the gas rate; between loading and flooding it rises quickly.

blocks.where: G<sub>design</sub> is the design gas mass flux in kg/(m²·s); G<sub>flood</sub> is the flooding gas mass flux at the same liquid rate, from the pressure-drop curve or the correlation in Chapter 3.7.

blocks.text: A liquid distributor at the top spreads liquid evenly over the whole cross-section. Holes, weirs or troughs feed the bed; a poor distributor gives dry channels and lost area. A redistributor every few metres of bed collects and re-spreads the liquid to undo maldistribution. A support plate at the bottom holds the packing with a large open area for gas and liquid.

HETP, height equivalent to a theoretical plate, is the bed height that does one equilibrium stage; it is measured for a packing and used to size towers. The stage calculation was in Chapter 3.5; packed design with HTU and NTU is in Chapter 3.7.

examples.question: A packed tower of 1.2 m inside diameter holds two 2 m beds of 25 mm rings (4 m of packing in all) with a redistributor between them. The packing has a = 200 m²/m³ and ε = 0.75. Find the total packing surface in the beds, the volume of voids, and the surface left if the packing is replaced by a 50 mm size with a = 100 m²/m³.
steps: Packed volume V<sub>bed</sub> = A<sub>c</sub>Z = 1.131 × 4 = 4.524 m³ (both beds; the redistributor gap holds no packing).
Packing surface with 25 mm rings = aV<sub>bed</sub> = 200 × 4.524 = 904.8 m².
Surface with 50 mm rings = 100 × 4.524 = 452.4 m². The loss is (904.8 − 452.4)/904.8 = 0.50, half the area.
examples.answer: The 25 mm beds have 904.8 m² of packing surface and 3.393 m³ of voids; 50 mm rings give 452.4 m², half the area (the wetted area is at most these values).

traps: Quoting the nominal size (say 25 mm) as if it were the specific area. A 25 mm ring has a specific surface of about 200 m²/m³, not 25 m²/m³.
Using the shell volume instead of the packed-bed volume. Disengaging space and distributors add shell height but not interfacial area.
Treating Fp as dimensionless. It has units of m⁻¹ (older charts use ft⁻¹), so convert before putting it into a correlation.
Confusing the loading point with the flooding point. Loading is the bend; flooding is the near-vertical turn-up. Design margin is set against flooding.
Reading the curves the wrong way: a higher liquid rate floods at a lower gas rate, not a higher one.

quiz.q: What does specific surface a measure, and what is its unit?
quiz.a: It is the surface area of the packing per unit volume of packed bed, in m²/m³. The wetted area, which does the actual transfer, is at most this value.

quiz.q: Name two random packings and one structured packing.
quiz.a: Random: Raschig rings and Pall rings (also Berl saddles, Intalox saddles). Structured: corrugated sheet packing (or wire gauze).

quiz.q: Why does specific surface a fall when the nominal packing size rises?
quiz.a: Larger pieces have less surface per unit volume. A 50 mm ring packs fewer pieces into the same bed volume than a 25 mm ring, so the wetted area per m³ of bed is lower.

quiz.q: Explain the loading point and the flooding point on a pressure-drop curve.
quiz.a: At the loading point the slope begins to rise because liquid accumulates in the voids. At the flooding point the curve turns almost vertical: liquid is held up and blown back, and the bed cannot pass the flows steadily.

quiz.q: A packed bed has diameter 2 m and depth 5 m. The packing has a = 150 m²/m³. Find the interfacial area.
Why is a packed tower designed at 50 to 70 % of the flooding gas rate rather than at flooding?
quiz.a: Operating at 50–70 % of the flooding gas mass flux leaves a 30–50 % margin, so small upsets in gas or liquid rate do not flood the bed. Near flooding the pressure drop and hold-up rise steeply and the bed becomes unstable: liquid is held up and blown back. The margin also covers errors in the flooding chart and in the packing factor.

quiz.q: Compare trays and packings for foaming service and for turndown.
quiz.a: Packings handle foaming service better because they agitate the liquid less than trays. Trays give better turndown: they can operate at lower liquid and gas rates, while a packed bed suffers from maldistribution when the liquid rate falls too far.

quiz.q: A packed bed of volume 4.0 m³ uses packing with ε = 0.70. Find the void volume.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern towers use structured packings with corrugated sheets, and newer designs use 3D-printed packing to tune area and pressure drop. CFD is used to study liquid maldistribution and to test distributor designs before a costly field trial. Search for 'Eckert generalized pressure drop correlation', 'packing factor Fp', 'HETP measurement packed column' and 'liquid maldistribution packed bed' if you want the research literature.
